title: The Resistance to Agency: Adoption Hurdles in Interactively Constructed Narratives
text:
Digital narrative construction, with its capacity for deep interactivity and variable authorial control, often faces systemic rejection despite demonstrable technical feasibility. The resistance stems less from the capability of the medium itself, and more from sociological friction points related to established cultural expectations of story consumption.

A primary point of inertia is the deeply ingrained psychological habit formed by decades of linear storytelling: the expectation that a narrative will follow an unfolding arc toward a singular climax. When complex, branching paths or high degrees of player agency are introduced, this model fails because users psychologically struggle with meaning fragmentation; they prefer the comfort and clarity of predetermined structure.

Furthermore, adoption resistance manifests as a fear—a subtle anxiety concerning the erosion of authorial intent. While the technology proves that limitless choices can be mapped onto a story world, audiences sometimes resist embracing narrative ambiguity. The expectation remains for a didactic or morally conclusive experience, leading them to reject narratives where meaning must be constructed and negotiated by the audience, rather than simply delivered.
